policy: A decision must name what was examined and carry conditions re-evaluated on every run. Having a control is not evidence that a requirement is met: no PASS may be inferred from the presence of MFA, RLS, CodeQL, an SBOM or a passing test. Anything without a valid, currently-holding decision stays PENDING and NOT_ASSESSED.

conditions.condition: React JSX still escapes interpolated values by default, so dangerouslySetInnerHTML remains the deliberate, auditable exception rather than the default
raw SQL access still goes through Prisma tagged templates rather than a string-built query

decisions.note: The two interpreters the application relies on most for output encoding both do it themselves, by default, at the point of use: React JSX escapes every interpolated value unless a component explicitly opts out with dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and Prisma parameterizes every value inside a Prisma.sql or plain tagged-template call before it reaches PostgreSQL. The deliberate exceptions to both defaults are real and are tracked as their own specific findings below (V1.2.1 for unescaped XML building, V1.2.9/V1.2.10/V1.2.3 for the other encoding-adjacent gaps) rather than folded into this architectural PASS.

conditions.condition: the shared escaper still encodes the three characters that change element structure, rather than deleting them
every free-text field in the ministry report still goes through the escaper
the financial-monitoring report still escapes the organisation identifiers it carries
the CSV reports still quote through the shared cell rather than by hand
no report builder interpolates a free-text deal field into XML unescaped again

decisions.note: buildMshXml, buildRosfinXml and buildRosstatCsv in exports.service.ts interpolated deal fields into an outgoing regulatory document with plain template literals and no encoding of any kind. culture and region are free-text String? columns on the Deal model, not enums, so a deal whose culture read a closing tag followed by another element did not produce a report describing that culture - it produced a different document, addressed to a ministry. The same file's Rosstat CSV wrote a culture into a quoted field without doubling the quote, which ends the field early and shifts every column after it. Two facts shaped this. First, an encoder that deleted metacharacters would also defeat injection while filing a report that disagrees with the database, so every case asserts both that the structure is unchanged and that decoding the field returns the original value byte for byte; the deleting variant fails 5 of the 11. Null and undefined now render as an empty element rather than as the words null and undefined, which is what the template literal wrote. Characters XML 1.0 cannot carry are dropped rather than escaped, because no entity represents them and a parser rejects the document either way. Second, and recorded here because it is a real limitation rather than a tidy result: this repository already escaped XML correctly. The FGIS-Grain codec has escapeXmlText and escapeXmlAttribute, private to that file, which is precisely how the export builders came to be written without them - the control existed and was reachable from one place only. The right answer is one implementation, and it was written and then reverted. The pc-crop-08c gate enforces an immutable scope: any change touching apps/api/src/modules/regulatory-integration/fgis-grain must contain only that contour's files, and it correctly refused a pass that also carried the export builders and this decision file. So there are two escaping implementations in the tree right now. That is stated rather than glossed, the convergence is raised as #4806 to be done inside the PC-CROP-08C scope where it belongs, and this decision claims only what the export path does. The CSV cell additionally prefixes a leading =, +, - or @ with an apostrophe: the file is well-formed with or without it, but the injection happens in the spreadsheet that opens it, and the reader here is a regulator. That guard marks a negative number too, which is the named cost and is taken knowingly, since a reader cannot tell -1 from a payload by its first character either. Mutation results: returning culture to raw interpolation fails 3 of 11, deleting instead of encoding fails 5, dropping the CSV quote doubling fails 2, dropping the formula guard fails 2. Separately recorded and not claimed here: the codec's FORBIDDEN_CONTROL_CHARACTER refusal is protected by no test on its reachable inbound path, found by mutation while confirming the reverted refactor preserved behaviour, and raised as #4801.

conditions.condition: the scheme check still runs first on every outbound attempt, before any address work
both untrusted-destination call sites still route through the guard rather than calling fetch directly
credentials in an outbound URL are still refused rather than sent

decisions.note: A partner registers a webhook URL through the partner API and this application later fetches it. The URL was stored verbatim: the endpoint declares its body as an inline TypeScript type, which erases to Object at runtime, so ValidationPipe skipped the parameter and no validator ever saw the field. Reachability was established before anything was changed, and it corrected the earlier record. That record named one fetch site, WebhookDispatcherService.dispatch, and a grep for callers finds none anywhere in the tree - the method is exported from its module but nothing invokes it. The fetch a partner can actually reach is in the controller's test endpoint, POST webhooks/:id/test, and it was not named. So the requirement was failing on a path the evidence did not mention, which is the same failure mode as the requirement itself. The check is applied at three points, not one: at registration, so a bad scheme is refused at the door; in the test endpoint, because that is the live path; and in the dispatcher, because a subscription stored before this existed has never been through registration and refusing at the point of use makes that safe without a data migration. http is on the allowlist deliberately. This requirement asks that the scheme be of a safe kind and names javascript: and data:; transport confidentiality is V12, and narrowing to https alone would break every partner already registered over http, which is a product decision rather than this control's to make. That choice is written down rather than left implied by an omission. What is deliberately not claimed: this does not decide where the URL points. Loopback, link-local and private ranges still pass, and the test suite asserts that they do, so the boundary is visible in the suite and not only in prose. Blocking them, and the DNS rebinding that defeats a naive version of it, is server-side request forgery under V1.3.6, which stays FAIL. Mutation results at the time this was closed: removing the guard from the reachable fetch failed 8 of 22, removing it from registration failed 9, removing the allowlist failed 8, removing it from the dispatcher failed 1. The two call sites have since been moved from a bare fetch onto the SSRF guard for V1.3.6, which begins with this same scheme check, so the conditions here name that entry point rather than the fetch call that no longer exists. The scheme check remains a separate control from the address rules and is credited separately: it proves the URL is of a safe kind, and V1.3.6 proves where it may point.

conditions.condition: the escaping helper used for dynamic JSON-LD content still exists and still escapes the script-breakout character

decisions.note: safeJsonLd(value) in apps/web/lib/gekta/seo.ts is JSON.stringify(value).replace(/</gu, \u003c) - the standard, correct mitigation for breaking a script tag via a literal < inside JSON-LD content - and it is the function used on the one page in the codebase that embeds database-sourced content this way (the Gekta topic pages). Two other pages (PlatformV7StructuredData.tsx and platform-v7/head.tsx) embed JSON-LD via the same dangerouslySetInnerHTML-plus-JSON.stringify pattern without the escaping helper, but both were read in full: every field in both objects is a hardcoded literal or a constant brand-origin URL, with no database or request-derived content anywhere in either. There is no live injection path today. Named rather than left implicit: this is an inconsistency worth closing (use safeJsonLd() everywhere this pattern appears, not just where it currently matters) so that the safety does not depend on both pages staying static forever - but it does not fail the requirement as it stands, since no untrusted data reaches either unescaped call site.

conditions.condition: no call site in the API still uses the unparameterized Prisma raw-query variants
no call site still uses Prisma.raw() to interpolate an unparameterized identifier or fragment into a tagged-template query
raw SQL access is still expressed through Prisma tagged templates, which parameterize every interpolated value

decisions.note: The application uses parameterized queries throughout. 73 files call $queryRaw or $executeRaw, and every one of them does so as a tagged template (Prisma.sql`...` or a plain template literal), which Prisma parameterizes automatically - a scan for the two unparameterized escape hatches Prisma exposes, $queryRawUnsafe/$executeRawUnsafe and Prisma.raw() (which bypasses parameterization for whatever is interpolated inside it, typically identifiers), returns zero matches across apps/api/src. Everywhere else, the ORM layer (Prisma Client's generated query builder) parameterizes by construction.

conditions.condition: the child_process module is still never imported by any runtime (non-test) file in the API, under either module specifier form

decisions.note: The deployed API never executes an operating-system command. A scan for every way the child_process module can be imported (bare and node:-prefixed specifiers, ESM import and CommonJS require) across non-test files in apps/api/src returns zero matches. The condition was corrected twice on review, both times by real findings: the first pass checked only the unprefixed specifier and two synchronous calls, missing the node:child_process form and async spawn/fork; broadening it to a bare .exec( substring then matched RegExp.prototype.exec() calls elsewhere (pattern.exec(pending) and similar), and separately, scanning all files rather than only runtime ones matched a legitimate test-only import - rls-transaction.service.spec.ts imports execFileSync from node:child_process to shell out during a test fixture, which never runs in the deployed process and is not part of the applications attack surface. The condition now keys on the module import itself (avoiding the call-shape false positive) restricted to non-test files (avoiding the test-fixture false positive), which is what the claim - the deployed API never shells out - actually means.

conditions.condition: the substitution builds no regular expression from input at all - the pattern is a module constant and the template is scanned once, with each field name looked up in a map
no RegExp is constructed anywhere in this file, so no key can become pattern syntax
the platform-set fields are written after the sender’s, so neither can be overridden
the hash is placed at the remembered position of its own field rather than at the first occurrence of the sentinel string

decisions.note: Closed by removing the class rather than escaping the input. The loop built new RegExp(`\\{\\{${key}\\}\\}`, 'g') once per key of the request body, with the braces escaped and the key not, and the reachability was traced rather than assumed: documents.controller.ts declares @Body() variables: Record<string, string | number>, an inline TypeScript type that erases at runtime, so ValidationPipe sees no class and the sender chooses both the property names and the values. The controller sits behind RolesGuard, so an authenticated user of any tenant is enough. Four separate defects were proven by running them, not argued: a key of `.*` rewrote every field of the document at once; a value of $` spliced the document text preceding the match into the field, because the second argument of .replace() interprets $&, $`, $' and $n; a key of (.*)*x against an ordinary 1901-character contract did not finish in 120 seconds, and Node being single-threaded that is the whole API process for that pod, not one slow request; and content.replace('PLACEHOLDER', hash) took the first occurrence of the string anywhere, so a sender whose field appeared earlier than the hash field took the hash and left the literal PLACEHOLDER in the document's own hash line. A fifth followed from the shape of the loop: substitution was iterative, so a value could introduce a placeholder that a later key then filled. The template is now scanned once against a module-constant pattern and each field name is looked up in a map, which removes all five: nothing is compiled from input, values are concatenated rather than used as a replacement string, and no substituted text is rescanned. The hash semantics are deliberately unchanged - it is still computed over the document carrying the literal sentinel in its hash field - because changing it would invalidate every previously issued document; a test pins that value. The service had no test of any kind before this. Mutations: restoring the original loop makes the suite hang rather than fail, which is the production symptom itself; placing the hash by first string occurrence fails the sentinel test; letting the sender's values win over the platform-set fields fails the override test.

conditions.condition: the cell still guards every character this requirement names, including tab and NUL
the guard is still applied to the first character and still prefixes an apostrophe
RFC 4180 quoting still doubles an embedded quote rather than dropping it
all three CSV producers still render through the shared cell rather than quoting by hand
no CSV producer builds a quoted field by hand again

decisions.note: Three CSV producers exist in exports.service.ts and all three were read. Two of them - the deal export and the ledger export - did double an embedded quote per RFC 4180 section 2.7, which was real and was credited, but neither escaped a leading =, +, -, @, tab or NUL, which this requirement names in addition to RFC 4180. The third, the Rosstat culture summary, did not even double quotes: it wrote a free-text culture into a quoted field directly, so a culture containing a quote ended the field early and shifted every column after it. All three now render through one csvCell, which encloses every field, doubles embedded quotes, and prefixes an apostrophe when the first character is one of the six this requirement lists. The trigger set is the requirement's own list plus carriage return, because some readers strip a leading CR and expose the character behind it. The guard marks a negative number too. That is the named cost and it is taken knowingly: a spreadsheet cannot distinguish the quantity -1 from a payload beginning with a minus sign either, so the alternative is not a cleaner report but an unprotected one. The apostrophe is deliberately visible rather than the character being deleted, because silently changing a value in a regulatory report is worse than a visible mark. Mutation results: removing the quote doubling fails 2 of the 11 cases, removing the formula guard fails 2. This requirement is credited only for CSV and formula injection; the XML side of the same file is V1.2.1, and the two were fixed in the same pass because they are the same defect in two output formats.

conditions.condition: loopback, link-local, private, CGNAT, unique-local and multicast are still refused by the address policy
IPv6 forms that carry an IPv4 address inside are still unwrapped and judged on what is inside
every resolved address is checked, not only the first
the connection is pinned to the vetted address, so a second resolution cannot be substituted
every redirect hop goes through the whole check again
both untrusted-destination call sites still go through the guard rather than calling fetch directly
neither untrusted-destination call site has gone back to a bare fetch

decisions.note: The outbound surface was inventoried before anything was written, because the policy depends on which destinations are actually needed. Thirteen fetch call sites exist in apps/api. Eleven take a destination the operator chose: ML_SERVICE_URL, VAULT_ADDR, the object storage endpoint, the two AI services which already check an explicit host allowlist, and the Telegram and VK endpoints which are constants. Two take a destination an outside party chose: the partner webhook dispatcher and the controller's test endpoint. That split decides the shape of the control. A blanket policy over every outbound call would refuse ml-service:8001 and vault:8200, which resolve into private space by design and were chosen by the operator - it would break real integrations while protecting nothing. The guard is therefore on the two untrusted-destination sites and nowhere else, and that is a deliberate boundary rather than an oversight. A second inventory fact shaped the compatibility choice: webhook subscriptions live in an in-memory Map with no Prisma model and no persistence, so no subscription survives a restart and there is no durable partner integration for a strict policy to break. Even so, the default is not a host allowlist - a partner endpoint is by nature an arbitrary address on the public internet, and a default-deny host list would make the feature unusable. The default is the category: public unicast only. PARTNER_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS narrows it further when an operator wants that, and an entry may name a host or a host:port, which is the ports dimension this requirement enumerates. Paths are deliberately unconstrained: the path is the partner's own endpoint, and reaching an arbitrary path on a public server is not SSRF against this application. Ports are unconstrained by default for the same reason - every internal destination is already removed by the address rules, so a port restriction on a public address protects nothing while breaking partners on non-standard ports. Three properties hold together and each defeats a different attack. Every resolved address is checked, not the first, because a name can carry a public A record and a loopback one and the attacker picks. The socket is pinned to the address that was vetted via the lookup hook, so there is no second resolution between check and connect for rebinding to poison. Every redirect hop is re-vetted from the scheme onward, because a 302 is a new destination chosen by the same party. Everything else refuses: an unparseable address, a failed or empty resolution, a redirect without a location, too many redirects, a transport error. Octal, hexadecimal and integer spellings of an address are refused rather than given a second interpretation, since a resolver may read 0177.0.0.1 as loopback. Six mutations are caught: checking only the first resolved address fails 1 of 180, re-resolving at connect time fails 1, following a redirect without re-vetting fails 3, dropping the literal-address check fails 2, dropping IPv4 link-local fails 9, and dropping the IPv4-mapped IPv6 unwrapping fails 4. Refusals are distinguishable from connection failures by their code, so a case cannot pass by failing to connect to something it should have refused.

conditions.condition: no template-execution engine dependency still exists in the API package manifest

decisions.note: The application never builds an executable template from untrusted input - no template-execution engine (Handlebars, EJS, Pug, Mustache, Nunjucks) is a dependency. document-template.service.ts performs a literal {{key}} text substitution, not template compilation or execution; the defect in how it builds that substitution's RegExp is a real, separate finding recorded under V1.2.9 and V1.3.12, not a template-injection issue as this requirement defines it.

decisions.note: The application has no memcache integration - no memcache client library is a dependency. There is no memcache-injection surface for this requirement to protect.

conditions.condition: the application still uses no printf-style format-string API

decisions.note: The classic format-string vulnerability class (a user-controlled value passed as a printf format specifier, letting %n and similar directives read or write arbitrary memory) requires a printf-family API operating on raw memory. Node.js/TypeScript has no such API in this codebase - no sprintf-style formatter is used - so there is no format-string surface for this requirement to protect.

conditions.condition: the SMTP client still rejects CR, LF and NUL in header values before sending
header values are still passed through an ASCII-safe encoder before being placed on the wire

decisions.note: auth-mail-smtp.ts explicitly guards against SMTP/IMAP-style header injection: header-value assembly rejects any value containing \r, \n or \0 before it is used, the sender/recipient address validator separately rejects \r\n\0< and >, and encodeHeader() is applied to values (such as the display name) placed into the Subject and From headers. This is deliberate, verified protection, not an absence of attack surface.

conditions.condition: no repository-wide backtracking or ReDoS analysis exists: no such tool is declared in any manifest, so the requirement’s general claim is unestablished whatever the traced instance does

decisions.note: The traced instance is closed in #4835 and this requirement still fails, which is the point of recording it separately. That instance was real and was proven by running it: a key of (.*)*x fed into a per-key RegExp did not finish against an ordinary 1901-character contract in 120 seconds, and Node being single-threaded that stops every request on the pod. The substitution now compiles nothing from input, so that path is gone. What is not established is the requirement's other half - that the application's regular expressions are free from elements causing exponential backtracking. Sixteen further new RegExp call sites exist under apps/api/src and apps/web/lib, none of them examined in this pass, and no backtracking-analysis tool is declared in any manifest, so there is no sweep to point at. Claiming PASS here on the strength of one closed instance would be exactly the substitution this programme forbids: a requirement answered with the evidence of a different, narrower one. The condition therefore watches for the sweep rather than for the instance - adding such a tool revokes this decision and forces the verdict to be taken again.

conditions.condition: the application is still implemented entirely in memory-managed TypeScript/JavaScript with no native or unmanaged code in application source

decisions.note: The application is written entirely in TypeScript running on Node.js/V8, a garbage-collected, memory-managed runtime with no raw pointer arithmetic or manual memory copying available to application code. There is no native addon (.node binary), FFI binding or node-gyp build anywhere in application source. This requirement targets memory-unsafe languages and unmanaged code, which this codebase does not contain.

conditions.condition: the tariff endpoint still takes distanceKm/weightTons as a plain, undecorated type literal rather than a class-validator DTO, so no range check runs before the multiplication
the service still multiplies those two values directly into a kopeck amount with no prior range or sign check

decisions.note: Corrected on review: the original version of this decision reasoned that JavaScript numbers do not wrap around the way fixed-width C integers do, and concluded the requirement does not apply to this runtime at all. That is too broad - the requirement is about sign, range and input validation preventing unsafe arithmetic results, and this codebase has a concrete, live instance of exactly that being skipped. POST tariff in route-planner.controller.ts declares its body as a plain type literal, { distanceKm: number; weightTons: number; vehicleType?: ... }, not a class-validator DTO class - the application does have a global ValidationPipe (main.ts), but class-validator only enforces decorators on an actual class, and there is none here, so nothing validates these two numbers before they reach the service. estimateLogisticsTariff() in route-planner.service.ts multiplies them directly - Math.round(distanceKm * weightTons * ratePerTonKmKopecks) - with no sign or range check first. A caller can submit a negative, non-numeric-after-coercion, or extremely large distanceKm/weightTons and get a nonsensical, negative, NaN or Infinity tariff back with no rejection. The BigInt usage this decision originally cited (deal version numbers, money in kopecks in the settlement path) is real and still a good pattern, but it does not cover this endpoint, so it cannot support a blanket NOT_APPLICABLE for the requirement as a whole.

conditions.condition: the application is still implemented entirely in a garbage-collected runtime with no manual memory release or raw pointers in application code

decisions.note: Node.js/V8 garbage-collects all application-level objects; there is no free(), no manual pointer management, and therefore no dangling-pointer or use-after-free class of defect reachable from application TypeScript. This requirement targets unmanaged memory, which this codebase does not have.

conditions.condition: the custom FGIS XML parser still rejects any named entity reference beyond the five predefined XML entities and numeric character references

decisions.note: The one XML parser in the codebase that handles incoming (externally-sourced) XML - a hand-written parser for FGIS grain-exchange documents, not a general-purpose library - has no DOCTYPE or ENTITY declaration handling anywhere in its 1457 lines: it implements no DTD-subset parsing at all. Its entity-reference resolution is a hard allowlist of the five predefined XML entities plus decimal and hex numeric character references; any other named entity is explicitly rejected with INVALID_ENTITY_REFERENCE (Named entity &...; is forbidden), read directly from the source rather than inferred. A parser with no mechanism to declare or resolve an external (SYSTEM/PUBLIC) entity cannot be made to fetch one - this is a structural absence of the XXE attack surface, not a configuration flag that happens to be off today.

conditions.condition: no unsafe deserialization library still exists in the API package manifest

decisions.note: The application deserializes untrusted input with JSON.parse and nothing else - no YAML loader, no node-serialize or unserialize-style library is a dependency. JSON.parse builds plain data objects and cannot itself instantiate arbitrary classes or execute code, which is the mechanism the deserialization attacks this requirement targets rely on; there is no unsafe deserialization surface here.

conditions.condition: validation is implemented in code, so a document has something to describe
the security documentation set still defines no input validation rules

decisions.note: Validation is implemented but undocumented. Neither the threat model nor the security policy defines how data items are checked against an expected structure, so there is no stated rule an implementation could be measured against. This condition watches those two documents; a rules document added elsewhere would need this decision revisited.

conditions.condition: the platform combines related data items whose consistency would have to be defined
no document defines the logical or contextual consistency expected of combined data items

decisions.note: The code enforces real cross-entity consistency, but no document states what consistency is expected. An undocumented rule cannot be reviewed, and a reviewer cannot tell an intended rule from an accidental one.

conditions.condition: no document states business logic limits, per-user or global

decisions.note: No documented expectation exists for business logic limits, either per user or across the application. This is the gap that also makes V2.3.2 unverifiable.

conditions.condition: cross-entity consistency is enforced on at least the lab finalisation command

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment deliberately not claimed. On the lab finalisation command the check is exemplary: the sample must belong to the deal and the tenant, its chain of custody must be complete, the signed evidence must be purpose-bound to that sample, shipment, acceptance, lab and protocol number, and the actor must hold signatory authority at that moment. The other commands in the policy table have not been examined, so the requirement is not claimed as met for the application.

conditions.condition: every command declares the status it may be issued from and the roles that may issue it
the authoritative path rejects a command issued from any other status

decisions.note: Deal actions are declared with an explicit from/to pair, and the PostgreSQL authority path rejects any command whose stored status does not match definition.from - inside the transaction that already holds the advisory lock, so the check cannot be raced. This decision covers that authoritative path. A second, different transition map exists in runtime-core/runtime-state-machine.ts, used only by runtime-core.service.ts; it is not what this PASS rests on.

conditions.condition: there is still no documented limit for an implementation to be measured against

conditions.condition: the canonical query is still sorted by byte value, without which the signed URL is rejected by the storage

the value is still an attachment and control characters are still removed from the filename

decisions.note: Uploaded bytes never pass through this application: a download is a presigned URL straight to object storage, and getDownloadUrl generated one with no response-content-disposition. Whether an uploaded .html or .svg rendered in the browser was therefore decided entirely by the bucket's own default configuration, which is not in version control and could not be checked from the repository. This requirement names the attachment disposition type as one control that satisfies it, and the presigned URL is the only place the decision can be made, so the override is set there. Three things had to be true rather than one. The parameter is folded into the signed canonical query rather than appended afterwards: an unsigned response override can simply be deleted by whoever holds the link, which would hand the decision straight back to the bucket, and a case asserts the signature differs with and without it. The filename is built rather than interpolated - sanitizeFilename runs at upload time and already removes control characters and quotes, but a record written before it existed has not been through it, and a filename reaching a header is where a stray CR stops being cosmetic. Both parameter forms are emitted because filenames here are routinely Cyrillic and the ASCII fallback cannot represent them; a case decodes the RFC 5987 form back to the exact original. Writing the tests surfaced a real defect in the signing code that had been invisible until now: the canonical query was sorted with localeCompare, and SigV4 requires byte ordering. Every existing parameter starts with X-Amz-, where the two orderings coincide, so nothing had ever exposed it; a lowercase response override sorts before X-Amz-Algorithm under localeCompare and after it by byte value, so the storage would have rebuilt a different canonical string and rejected the signature. The sort is corrected and a condition above forbids the regression. Scope of the claim: after this, every path that serves bytes to a browser sets an attachment disposition - the compliance and exports controllers already did for their generated CSV and XML, where the filename is application-generated - and main.ts sets X-Content-Type-Options nosniff on API responses. Mutations: appending the override after signing fails 3 of 21, restoring localeCompare fails 1, removing the override from the service fails 2, and keeping control characters in the filename fails 1. The service cases exist because the first version of this suite exercised only the primitive and the adapter: a getDownloadUrl that stopped supplying the override left every case green, which is the same hole this programme found in the cursor-key pass.

conditions.condition: the shared base tsconfig still disables strict type checking for the whole monorepo

decisions.note: Corrected on review: the original version of this decision credited assertCsrf() (server-request-security.ts) as this application's CSRF defence and cited its use in a large number of route files as evidence of broad coverage. That mechanism is real and, where it is used, correctly implemented (same-origin check, double-submit cookie, constant-time comparison) - but coverage is the actual question this requirement asks, and it is not comprehensive. decisions.note: Corrected: the previous decision assessed a different requirement. Its note described SSRF - "an authenticated partner can point a webhook at an internal service or a cloud metadata endpoint" - and V4.2.5 does not ask that. It asks that an application which builds and sends requests avoid creating URIs or header fields too long for the receiving component to accept, because an over-length request line or header field is answered with 414 or 431 every time and becomes a denial of service. The SSRF property is real and was closed separately in #4805 and #4816; borrowing it as this requirement's evidence meant V4.2.5 had never been assessed against its own text at all. Worth recording how that survived: this decision carried a self-revoking FAIL condition, and it did not revoke when the SSRF gap was closed. The condition watched the dispatcher for the words isprivate, allowlist, assertpublic and new url(, and the fix that landed uses none of them - it calls safeOutboundRequest. So the condition went on holding while the thing it described had been fixed. A revocation check written against vocabulary rather than behaviour fails in the direction that keeps a verdict alive after it stopped being true, which is worse than failing loudly. Assessed properly, V4.2.5 was still FAIL: nothing bounded the size of anything. The stored url is unbounded - the endpoint takes an inline { url: string } body type that no validation class acts on, per V2.2.1 - and the dispatcher built headers from stored values with no ceiling. Both are now bounded at the single place every outbound request passes, rather than where the value happens to be stored: a limit applied at registration is bypassed by any caller that builds a request from something else. The ceilings are the smallest documented limits among the servers a webhook is likely to reach rather than a preference of this application: nginx defaults to an 8 KiB request line and 8 KiB header buffers, so 2 KiB of URI and 4 KiB per header value inside an 8 KiB total stays acceptable to all of them. Both are measured in bytes, because a server counts octets and one Cyrillic character is two of them - on this platform that is not a corner case. The header check runs ahead of the redirect loop, since the header set does not change between hops and a refusal must precede the first connection. Five mutations, and one of them found a hole in these very tests: removing the URI ceiling fails 3 of 42, removing the header check fails 3, measuring the URI in characters fails 1, dropping the total-size check fails 1 - and measuring header VALUES in characters originally failed nothing at all. The byte-measurement case existed for the URI and not for headers, so the property the comment claimed was unasserted. It is asserted now, and that mutation fails.

decisions.note: Closed by bounding the read instead of trusting the declaration. The guard compared content-length against the ceiling, and two ordinary requests walked past it - both proven by running them rather than argued: a chunked request carries no content-length at all, so Number(null || '0') is zero and the comparison never fires; and a malformed value such as content-length: not-a-number yields NaN, so Number.isFinite(NaN) short-circuits the same comparison. The second was not in the recorded note and was found while measuring the first. Past the guard the route called request.formData(), which was measured buffering a 12 MiB body in 123 ms - the size becomes knowable only once the memory is already spent, on an endpoint that requires no authentication. The bound now counts bytes as they arrive and cancels the stream at the ceiling, so nothing the sender declares participates in the decision; the declared size survives only as a cheap refusal for an honest client. The stream is cancelled rather than abandoned, so a sender is not left writing into a socket nobody reads. Three mutations, each caught: removing the cancel, an off-by-one at the ceiling, and reverting the route to request.formData() - the last of which passes the type check and every reader-level test, which is why the route-level cases exist at all.

decisions.note: Closed against the requirement's own text, which asks for a check against maximum uncompressed size AND against maximum number of files BEFORE uncompressing. Both halves are present because neither is sufficient alone: the declared uncompressed size lives in the zip central directory at offset +24 and is written by the sender, so a check of it alone believes a liar; maxOutputLength alone spends memory up to the ceiling on a file that already declared itself unacceptable. The route is unauthenticated - /api/public-platform-assistant/attachments is listed in PUBLIC_API_EXACT - and DEFLATE reaches about 1032:1, so the 8 MiB the route accepts inflated to roughly 8 GiB inside the request handler. Three paths were unbounded: inflateRawSync for the docx member, inflateSync for every PDF FlateDecode stream in a loop, and the archive entry count, which was limited only by the uint16 the EOCD record can hold. The principle was already written down in this codebase for images - image-dimensions.ts, closed for V5.2.6, opens with the observation that the file-size limit bounds the input and not the decoder's output - and the route repeated it in a comment immediately above the two decoders that did not have it. The decompressors now live in the library rather than the route, so the route imports no zlib and has no way to inflate outside the budget; that is a structural guarantee and is recorded as one rather than as a behavioural claim. The PDF path distinguishes a corrupt stream, which is skipped because PDFs in the wild are partly damaged, from a budget refusal, which aborts extraction - without that distinction a sender packs a hundred bombs and each is caught and skipped in turn. The xlsx path is unzipped by ExcelJS, which cannot be stopped at a ceiling. Review on the PR found that leaving that format on the declared sizes alone was not a control at all: JSZip compares the declared size only after producing the decompressed data, so a two-byte lie in the central directory passed the pre-check and then inflated without a ceiling on a public endpoint. Corrected rather than argued with - xlsx entries are now inflated here under the same budget and the output discarded, which proves the directory did not lie and debits the budget by the bytes ExcelJS will then hold, without double-charging. Peak memory of the check itself is one entry. The same review found that the declared total was compared against the remaining budget but never deducted, so four archives each saw the full allowance; the inflate-verify pass is what debits it now. A route-level test proves both are reached rather than merely present. What is deliberately not claimed: V5.2.1 stays FAIL. With Transfer-Encoding: chunked there is no content-length, Number(null || '0') is 0, the pre-check passes, and request.formData() buffers the whole body; that is a different defect in the body-reading path and needs streaming byte accounting, not a decompression ceiling. Mutations, each caught: dropping maxOutputLength fails 2, letting the PDF path swallow a budget refusal fails 1, removing the xlsx pre-check wiring fails the route-level test, and returning a direct zlib import to the route fails the structural test.

decisions.note: Closed by routing the four file-serving routes through the builder that already existed. attachmentDisposition in common/security was written for V3.2.1 and does exactly what this requirement asks - it strips path separators, removes control characters, escapes quotes in the ASCII form and emits the RFC 5987 filename* alongside - and the export and compliance routes interpolated their own header instead. The control existed, was correct, sat in common/security, and the places that needed it did not call it. Reachability was established rather than assumed: only exports.controller.ts's ledger route takes user input, @Param('dealId'), and exportLedgerCsv does not reject an unknown id - assertExportRole checks the role only, findMany({ where: { dealId } }).catch(() => []) turns any string into an empty result set, and the route answers 200. So any user holding an export role puts an arbitrary string into the header. Proven by running it: a dealId of x"; filename="ledger.csv.exe produced a header carrying two filename parameters, which is a download-name spoof, and a Cyrillic dealId went into the header raw with no filename* - and Cyrillic names are the ordinary case on this platform. Deliberately not claimed: CRLF was not exploitable here, because Node rejects control characters in a header value with ERR_INVALID_CHAR; the builder strips them anyway so the route returns a file rather than a 500. The two routes with no user input were moved as well, because the requirement is about how a served name is encoded rather than where it came from. What is not addressed and is recorded separately: exportLedgerCsv and exportDealsCsv carry no tenant predicate at all, and whether the row-level policy named ledger_select_all closes that path is unestablished - that is a V8 authorization question needing a live-database pass, not something to settle in passing.

conditions.condition: every route that serves a file builds the header through the shared builder rather than by hand

decisions.note: This requirement asks for a document, so a document is the control - and the reason it was FAIL is that the document was not merely missing, it was wrong. A survey of every file in the tree that signs a session token or writes a session cookie found twelve surfaces. The one pathway the previous evidence named, the gov-id bridge, mints nothing at all: its callback validates state against a cookie, then redirects to a fallback target with a reason and clears its own cookies, never exchanging the authorization code and never writing a session, access, refresh or CSRF cookie. Five real pathways were unnamed: three demo-login routes plus a proxy branch; the owner cabinet open at /platform-v7/staff/open-cabinet; /api/platform-v7/cabinet-session; /api/platform-v7/cabinet-lock-login; and the Gekta registration email verification, which mints an enrolment session from a one-time token. All of them are controlled - no open door was found. Demo login is fail-closed because demoLoginAllowed checks NODE_ENV before it reads its enabling flag, its token is not a signed JWT and the API accepts exactly one format, and the web proxy refuses to forward it. Cabinet lock login answers 410 in production before reading its own configuration. The owner cabinet open, the one cabinet route reachable in production, requires a CSRF token compared in constant time plus an allow-listed origin, an existing access cookie, and then either an API-confirmed ACTIVE PLATFORM_OWNER assignment with MFA already verified - a higher bar than ordinary login clears - or a fixture token gated behind three environment variables including a hard expiry, whose claim names a real access token does not carry; the role is bound server-side to a fixed controlled test organization. So the finding was never that these are weak. It was that the security record did not know they existed, which is exactly what this requirement is about. THREAT_MODEL.md now carries the inventory with the proof and the strength for each entry and a separate list of surfaces that are not ways in - refresh, MFA step-up, the staff-access header, the gov-id bridge and the removed Sber callback. It is PASS on a document only because the document is held to the tree: scripts/security/verify-authentication-pathways.test.mjs enumerates every minting surface and fails when one is not accounted for, and fails again when a named pathway leaves the document. Both directions are mutation-checked. Whether the controls behind those twelve surfaces are enforced CONSISTENTLY is the separate second half of V6.3.4, which stays FAIL and is not claimed here. Raised as #4780.

conditions.condition: the format upgrade still does not present itself as a credential change: no version bump, no session revocation, no notification
legacy bcrypt is still verified, so no existing account is locked out

decisions.note: bcryptjs truncates its input at 72 bytes. Against a policy maximum of 128 characters that leaves 56 of them out of the hash, and for Cyrillic, where a character is two UTF-8 bytes, the effective limit arrives at 36 characters - inside the length the registration form promises. The versioned scheme, the legacy verify and verifyPasswordWithUpgrade were all written in an earlier pass and were correct. Nothing called them. Both login paths used verifyPassword, which cannot rewrite anything, so not one stored bcrypt hash was ever upgraded and the truncation stayed in place for every existing account: the control existed and was reachable from nowhere, which is the failure mode this programme keeps finding. Both paths now verify through the upgrading form, and a test asserts the wiring rather than assuming it. The profile was re-decided against the primary source rather than kept. The earlier value, N=2^16 r=8 p=1, was chosen for equivalence with the bcrypt cost already configured - a basis that measures what was already there rather than what is recommended - and it appears nowhere on the ladder OWASP publishes. That source names Argon2id first, scrypt when Argon2id is unavailable, and bcrypt for legacy only; for scrypt it lists N=2^17 (128 MiB) r=8 p=1 at the top, trading memory for parallelism down to N=2^13 r=8 p=10. Argon2id is not available in Node without a new dependency, which would open licence, provenance, SBOM and vulnerability review, so scrypt is taken as that same source's sanctioned alternative and the top rung is used. The memory question was settled by measurement, not by preference. 128 MiB per verification sounds unbounded under load and is not: scrypt runs on the libuv threadpool, four wide by default, so at most four verifications are in flight whatever the queue depth. Measured here, peak process RSS was 558 MiB at four concurrent verifications and 559 MiB at thirty-two - the burst becomes latency, not memory exhaustion. The ceiling is proportional to UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, and the production VPS core count is not checked from here, so 560 MiB is a measured ceiling on a four-core machine rather than a promise about a specific host. The write path needed a database function because public.users is under FORCE row level security, and FORCE means a SECURITY DEFINER function owned by the table owner is still subject to the policies. That was found by running it rather than by reading: the first version returned false for a legitimate upgrade because the UPDATE's WHERE clause reads passwordHash and no SELECT policy admitted the authority. The authority is dedicated rather than borrowed from the password-reset role, and its privilege is column-scoped to passwordHash, so the row policy decides which rows and the column grant decides which fields. The function deliberately does not touch credential_version or password_changed_at and sends no notification: a format upgrade is not a credential change, and revoking every session or raising a false security alert because the server re-encoded a password the user did not change would be worse than the truncation. A failed rewrite never turns a correct password into a refusal - the password was verified before the attempt - and the next login tries again. No bulk migration and no forced reset: a hash is only rewritten when the user proves the password. Production rollout remains a separate exact-SHA release with its own authority, and production PASS is not claimed. One note on how that last property is checked, because the first attempt at it was wrong in a way this programme has now hit several times: the condition originally asserted the absence of the words credential_version and password_changed_at, and it was rejected immediately - by the comment above the function, which names both columns to say it does not write them. The evaluator reads raw text, comments included, so an absence check written against a word measures the prose, not the code. It now names statements instead: SET of either column, any reference to auth.credential_states at all, the session-revocation functions, and the mail outbox. conditions.condition: the acceptance window is not widened to compensate for the stricter rule

decisions.note: verifyTotp accepted a code against three time steps and recorded nothing, so the same six digits verified again for as long as the window held. The boolean return was the reason the control could not exist: a verifier that knows a code is valid but not WHICH time step it belongs to has nothing to record. RFC 6238 section 5.2 states the rule in the verifier's own terms - an implementation MUST NOT accept a second attempt for a time step it has already accepted, and should reject any attempt whose step is not greater than the last one. matchTotpCounter now returns the counter, and a single conditional UPDATE on auth.credential_states consumes it. The predicate is the whole control. A read followed by a write would leave a window where two processes both see the old value and both accept the same code, and the API and the workers are separate processes, so that race is the one that matters rather than a theoretical one. The consume lives inside verifyMfaCode rather than in its three call sites, because a control each caller must remember to invoke is one a caller will eventually not invoke - which is how the matching backup-code path stayed correct while this one did not. There is no way to obtain a TOTP acceptance without having consumed it. Strictly greater, not greater-or-equal: the same rule that refuses a replayed counter also refuses an older counter still inside the acceptance window, which is the shape a replay actually takes. That distinction was verified against PostgreSQL 16 rather than asserted, and it matters: with <= the predicate 100 <= 100 holds and the replay is accepted. The first version of the unit suite could not see the difference, because its fake client implemented the comparison itself instead of executing the statement - it proved the fake correct, not the SQL. The cross-process race was proved the same way: twenty concurrent connections attempting the same counter, one accepted and nineteen refused. The column is nullable with no default and no backfill; an authenticator that has never completed a TOTP verification has no last counter, and inventing one would either lock out a legitimate first use or accept a replay of whatever the backfilled value implied. NULL is handled explicitly by the predicate. The acceptance window is unchanged at three steps, so this is single-use enforcement rather than a narrowed window; V6.5.5, which asks about the lifetime itself, is a separate question and is not claimed here. Backup codes and the opaque-token authority were already single-use and are untouched.

conditions.condition: backup codes are still stored through digestMfaBackupCode's keyed HMAC rather than a salted password-storage hash
newly minted codes still carry at least the 112 bits that make a standard hash the allowed option

decisions.note: Half of this requirement is now met and the half that is not is the reason the verdict stays FAIL. The requirement offers two ways to be compliant: a lookup secret below 112 bits of entropy must be kept under an approved password storage hash with a 32-bit random salt, or it must carry 112 bits or more, in which case a standard hash function is allowed. Backup codes are stored through opaque-token-authority.ts's digestMfaBackupCode, an HMAC-SHA256 keyed MAC, so the second route is the one this codebase has to take. It could not, because generateBackupCodes drew randomBytes(6) - 48 bits. #4776 raised the draw to base32Encode(randomBytes(15)) - 120 bits in 24 RFC 4648 characters with no padding - so every code minted from that commit onward is on the right side of the threshold, and mfaBackupCodeEntropy.spec.ts measures that on generated values rather than on the constant: lowering the draw back to six bytes fails three of its eight cases. Salting was considered and rejected on the merits rather than on cost. A salted hash cannot be looked up by value, so verification would have to try each of a user's stored codes in turn at password-hash cost - seconds of work per submitted attempt, none of it paid for by an attacker submitting garbage - where the keyed digest is one deterministic computation and one index lookup. Raising the secret buys the same compliance without that. What still fails: the requirement is about what is stored, and the codes stored before this change are 48-bit codes under that same keyed digest. They cannot be re-hashed, because a digest is all the backend has; the code itself is gone. They also cannot be told apart from new ones - the digest is fixed-width and carries no format - so the verifier accepts both, deliberately: a format check on input would lock every existing user out of their own recovery path without warning. So for any account enrolled before #4776 and not since re-enrolled, the stored secret is still under 112 bits under a standard hash, which is exactly what the requirement forbids. Moving this to PASS needs that population gone, by invalidating outstanding backup codes and forcing re-enrolment. The owner decided in #4777 not to, and the reasoning is recorded there rather than left implicit, because a residual accepted for a reason is not the same record as one nobody looked at. The entropy is not what defends these codes; the server-side digest key is, and in production that key is mandatory - the process refuses to start without AUTH_OPAQUE_TOKEN_DIGEST_KEY or AUTH_TOKEN_PEPPER. Against a database-only compromise, the scenario this threat model actually carries, 48 bits and 120 bits are equally safe: an HMAC cannot be brute-forced or searched by value without its key. Against a host compromise both are equally lost, since an attacker holding the signing secret mints access tokens directly and has no reason to attack a backup code. Online guessing is bounded by the challenge attempt counter regardless of entropy. The one scenario where 120 bits beats 48 is a leaked digest key together with a database dump but without the session-signing secret - narrow, and not what invalidation would be paid for. What it would be paid with is the platform owner's own recovery path: the existing reset acts on a membership and needs an administrator, and above the platform owner there is none, so burning printed codes removes the last rung of that ladder while bus factor 1 is still an open gap in the threat model. The population drains on its own instead - the stored set is rewritten on every code use and on re-enrolment - and if it is ever to be cleared on a schedule, the mechanism already exists and needs no new code: the admin MFA reset sets mfa_backup_hashes to NULL, clears the TOTP secret and issues a recovery credential to the verified address. It is recorded as FAIL and not as partial credit because the size of the affected population cannot be measured from the source tree, and this matrix does not read production data; nothing else in this matrix depends on it. A second backup-code generator was removed rather than left to drift: issueMfaBackupCodeCredential in the authority minted its own randomBytes(6) code with no runtime caller, beside the live generator. Raising entropy in one of two generators for the same purpose is how a stale number waits to be inherited by the next caller, so the issuer now takes the minted code and the entropy decision is made in exactly one place; the same test fails if the second generator comes back. The decorative apps/api/src/modules/mfa module referenced in earlier versions of this note was removed in #4688 and never persisted anything, so it was never evidence here.

Backup codes, OOB/MFA-recovery tokens, and registration/reset tokens are all likewise minted from Node's crypto.randomBytes via auth-crypto.ts or opaque-token-authority.ts; no Math.random() or other non-CSPRNG source was found generating any of these secrets.

The margin was already wide before #4776 raised the draw from six bytes (48 bits), so this verdict does not move; the condition does, because it named the six-byte draw and that draw no longer exists anywhere in the tree. Left as it was, it would have been rejected and this decision would have fallen silently to NOT_ASSESSED. decisions.note: Both ceilings this requirement sets are now enforced in runtime code and held there by tests that fail when either is widened. TOTP. verifyTotp checked a submitted code against three consecutive 30-second steps, which kept one code value acceptable for close to ninety seconds. It now checks the current step alone, so a code's lifetime is the 30 seconds the requirement allows. The implementation is checked against the RFC 6238 Appendix B published vectors through the real verifier, not against a copy of itself, so the six window assertions rest on an implementation independently shown to be correct. Restoring the wide window fails 4 of the 10 cases. This is a deliberate divergence from RFC 6238 s5.2, which recommends allowing at most one step of drift - that is, exactly what was there before. The two documents disagree and neither is wrong; this codebase takes the stricter bound, and the cost is recorded rather than hidden: a device whose clock is off by more than one step can no longer log in by TOTP. The otpauth URI handed to the authenticator app derives its period from the same constant, so what is advertised and what is enforced cannot drift apart. Out of band. MFA_RECOVERY_TTL_MS was 30 minutes and is now 10. No migration was needed: expires_at was already computed from the constant, and challenges minted earlier keep the expiry they were issued with and age out. The pending-MFA challenge window on both session services was already at the ceiling and is now held there by condition rather than by luck. The mail is the other half of the same claim, and it was the weaker half: the delivery type already carried expiresInSeconds and the copy ignored it, restating thirty minutes in three languages. The sentence is now a function of the delivered lifetime, clamped to the ceiling, so it can understate the lifetime but never overstate it, and a delivery arriving without one falls back to the ceiling rather than guessing. apps/api/src/modules/auth-mail/auth-mail-templates.ts holds an unreferenced second copy of the same mail; it is not deleted, because a template is not a control, but it now takes the lifetime as a required argument so a future caller cannot inherit a stale number. Scope, stated so the PASS is not read wider than it is. Narrowing the window is not replay protection: the same code presented twice inside its own step still verifies twice. That is V6.5.1, it needs durable per-user state, and it remains FAIL under #4682.
