conditions.condition: the policy still states every limit, names the constants that enforce them, and says what it does not cover
patterns: what this policy does not cover

conditions.condition: the idle limits the policy states are the ones the code enforces
the policy has not gone back to the rejected twelve-hour limit

decisions.note: Both limits are now written down with the reasoning behind them, and the document names the constants that enforce them so a reviewer checks it against the code rather than taking its word. The inactivity timeout is twelve hours and the absolute maximum is thirty days. The reasoning for twelve is recorded rather than asserted: shorter would be worked around rather than observed, because this platform is used by drivers, elevator operators and surveyors whose work is interrupted by the job rather than by choice, and an idle limit that ends a session mid-shift is met by keeping a tab awake - the same exposure with the control now being evaded instead of followed. Longer would leave a found or borrowed device carrying a live session for a season rather than a shift; sixty times shorter than the absolute cap is the property being bought. The document is also explicit that the idle limit does not stand alone in front of the operations that matter, because financial commands above a threshold already demand recently verified MFA regardless of session age. One honesty is recorded rather than smoothed: thirty days was in the code before it was in a document, so what is written is the reasoning that supports it, arrived at by reading which controls already invalidate a session - credential version change, membership deactivation, organization unverification, role removal - rather than a record of a review held at the time. The document says that about itself. It also says what it does not cover: concurrent session limits, which are neither defined nor enforced and leave V7.1.2 FAIL, and key lifecycle, which is a key management policy and leaves V11.1.1 FAIL. Revised after owner review: the twelve-hour limit this decision first recorded was rejected and replaced with one hour, and fifteen minutes for the roles ROLES_REQUIRING_MFA already names as privileged. The original justification argued that drivers and elevator operators are interrupted by the job, so a shorter limit would be worked around by keeping a tab awake. That argument was wrong in a way worth recording rather than deleting: it treated the session as the only way to preserve work in progress, when the answer to an interrupted shift is to keep the state and reauthenticate back into it. An idle limit chosen by how inconvenient logging in feels is set by the UX budget rather than by risk. The policy document keeps that history visible, because a policy that quietly replaces its own justification is the kind of record this programme keeps finding to be untrue. The privileged tier is decided from the role on the session context row being validated, so there is one authority for who is privileged rather than a second one built from staffRoles, and a malformed or absent role falls to the ordinary limit rather than to none. Product sessions carry a scope and not a platform role, so the tier does not apply there and is not faked.

conditions.condition: no concurrent-session limit is enforced in the session service
no document defines how many parallel sessions an account may hold

decisions.note: Neither the limit nor its documentation exists. An account may hold unlimited parallel sessions; organization-team.service.ts surfaces an activeSessionCount for display, which counts sessions rather than bounding them.

conditions.condition: the platform participates in a federated identity ecosystem as a relying party
no document covers session management for that federated participation

decisions.note: The platform is an OIDC relying party against a government identity provider, so it is part of a federated identity ecosystem and this requirement applies. No documentation covers how sessions in that ecosystem are created, timed out or terminated.

conditions.condition: both verification paths read the session from the database rather than trusting the token

decisions.note: Session verification is a backend database read on every request, on both paths. The token carries a session id; authority comes from the stored row. A client cannot assert its own session state, and revocation takes effect on the next request rather than at the next refresh. Unlike the two token verifiers assessed under V9, these two session paths agree - auth.service.ts is in fact stricter, adding membership status, organization verification and role validity.

conditions.condition: session and refresh identifiers are generated per authentication

decisions.note: Sessions are represented by dynamically generated reference tokens, not by anything derived from user data. Each authentication mints a fresh session id and a fresh refresh-token family id.

conditions.condition: reference token secrets come from a cryptographic random source
stored values are digests compared in constant time

decisions.note: A reference token is 32 random bytes with an 18 byte random identifier. Only an HKDF-derived digest is stored, and comparison is constant-time, so neither guessing nor a timing oracle nor a database read yields a usable token.

conditions.condition: authentication mints a new session rather than reusing one
the new session is unusable until the second factor completes

decisions.note: Each authentication creates a new session with a new identifier and a new refresh family, and the session starts in MFA_PENDING so the identifier issued before the second factor cannot be used as an authenticated one. Refresh rotates the credential on every use and reuse of a rotated token revokes the entire family.

conditions.condition: both session pathways still refuse a session idle beyond the limit, from one shared constant
the limit applied is selected by role rather than fixed for everyone
the product pathway still takes the limit from that constant rather than restating a number

decisions.note: The earlier verdict said there is no last-activity timestamp from which an inactivity timeout could be derived. There is, and there has been since the sessions table was created: auth.sessions.last_seen_at, maintained on every authenticated request through touchSession and throttled to one write a minute so it costs one UPDATE per session per minute rather than one per request. What was missing was a reader. Nothing enforced a limit against it, so a session left untouched stayed valid for the full thirty-day absolute lifetime - which is the gap this requirement is about, since an absolute cap does not bound idle exposure. The timestamp is now selected into the session context and checked in sessionInvalidReason, the single place every admitted request passes through, so the platform login, the refresh rotation and the MFA challenge path all inherit it without a second implementation; the product pathway checks the same way from the same exported constant, because two session stores with two idle rules would be exactly the inconsistency V6.3.4 is about. No schema change and no migration were needed - the column and its maintenance already existed, and the queries that build the context read auth.sessions inline rather than through a SECURITY DEFINER function, so only the SELECT list changed. The check runs before touchSession, so it reads the previous activity rather than the request making it, and an idle session is revoked with reason SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT rather than merely refused, so it does not have to be caught again. Twelve hours, with the risk reasoning recorded under V7.1.1. Three mutations fail the suite: removing the platform check, giving the product pathway its own literal, and widening the limit to the absolute cap. Limit revised on owner review from twelve hours to one hour, with fifteen minutes for ADMIN, COMPLIANCE_OFFICER and ARBITRATOR. Fifteen minutes matches the MFA freshness window already required for privileged operations, so the session and the step-up expire together rather than leaving a window where one is live and the other is not. Neither the financial step-up nor the control-plane step-up is relaxed to compensate for the shorter window.

conditions.condition: the absolute maximum is still thirty days and still set at creation rather than extended by use
the policy still records the absolute maximum and the honest provenance of its justification
patterns: the honest limit of this justification

decisions.note: The mechanical half was already met: the absolute maximum is set as expires_at at session creation and re-checked on every request, and activity does not extend it - which is what separates it from the inactivity timeout that activity does reset. It failed on the other half, that the limit follow risk analysis and documentation, because thirty days was stated nowhere and justified nowhere. It is now stated in docs/security/SESSION_POLICY.md with the reasoning: the re-authentication it forces puts a floor under how long a credential change, a role change or a device handover can go unreflected in a live session, and it is a backstop rather than the primary control, because a session is already invalidated immediately when the credential version changes, when the membership stops being active, when the organization stops being verified, or when the role becomes one the platform does not admit. The provenance of that justification is recorded rather than dressed up: thirty days was in the code before it was in a document, so what is written is reasoning arrived at by reading what the surrounding controls already enforce, not a record of a review held at the time. The document says so about itself, and says where a different number would go if a review reaches one. With V7.3.1 now enforced, the two limits do different work rather than one standing in for the other.

conditions.condition: a terminated session is refused on both paths

decisions.note: Termination is honoured on the next request, not the next token refresh, because both paths re-read session status from the database each time. A revoked or expired session yields no further access even while its access token is still within its 15 minute validity.

conditions.condition: a session belonging to a non-active user is refused
the platform path also refuses on membership and organization state

decisions.note: Disabling an account terminates its sessions in effect: every request re-reads user status and refuses anything that is not ACTIVE, then revokes the session. No separate sweep is needed, so there is no window in which a disabled account still holds a live session. The platform path additionally follows membership and organization state, which covers an employee removed from an organization rather than deactivated outright.

conditions.condition: a successful password change advances the credential version
a session minted under an older credential version is refused

decisions.note: A password change increments the credential version, and both session paths refuse any session whose recorded version no longer matches. Every other session ends immediately. Stated precisely: the application does not offer this as an option, it does it unconditionally, which exceeds what the requirement asks for. No option UI exists and none is claimed.

conditions.condition: the two authenticated surfaces without a logout control still have none
the logout control that exists is still rendered by nobody

decisions.note: Still FAIL, but two of the three surfaces the earlier note named were wrong and the correction matters more than the verdict. Under /platform-v7 the requirement is met and always was: the logout control lives in the header menu the protected shell renders, and the route-group layout applies it to every page beneath - including the staff plane, which sits under that same layout and therefore inherits it rather than lacking it. The platform-v7r runtime is not a surface at all: middleware answers every /platform-v7r path with a 308 redirect to the /platform-v7 equivalent, so its shell is never served to anyone and cannot be missing a control. What the earlier note did not name are the two surfaces that actually fail. /assistant renders through PageFrame, which renders AppChrome, and neither carries a logout control; it is gated to all authenticated roles, so it is squarely in scope. /gekta/console is the Gekta owner console, authenticated - it handles a 401 as authentication_required - and carries no logout control either. The component for this already exists and is the sharpest part of the finding: session-controls.tsx exports a SessionControls with a working logout button, and nothing in the tree renders it. Closing this means mounting a control on both surfaces, and the two contours log out through different endpoints - /api/auth/logout for the platform and the Gekta account path for the console - so it is two mounts rather than one. That is user-interface work rather than a change to a control's mechanism, and it is left for a pass that can verify what renders rather than being asserted from source here.

conditions.condition: an administrator can terminate another user sessions
the staff plane can review and revoke sessions

decisions.note: POST auth/sessions/revoke-user is restricted to ADMIN and terminates every session of the named user. The staff plane additionally offers permission-gated review of all active sessions and revocation of an individual one. The requirement asks for per-user or all-user termination; per-user exists and is enforced by role.

conditions.condition: the role change is implemented in this service
that service still requires no re-authentication for it
a wired fresh-MFA gate does exist elsewhere, so the capability is real

decisions.note: A fresh-MFA gate exists and is genuinely wired: registration-decision.service.ts refuses a review decision unless the reviewer verified MFA within 15 minutes, at three call sites. It is credited here because it shows the capability is real and invoked - unlike the signing-authority policy under V2.3.5, which has no callers at all. But it guards registration review, not account attributes. Changing an organization membership role is a sensitive attribute change and organization-invitation.service.ts applies no re-authentication to it - only rate limiting at the controller and an optimistic version check. The password path is different and defensible: there is no in-session password change endpoint, only a reset requiring an emailed token, which is itself a re-authentication.

conditions.condition: the staff plane lets a caller view and terminate their own sessions
the user-facing auth surface offers no equivalent

decisions.note: Staff can view their active sessions and revoke one. Ordinary platform users cannot: the only session-termination endpoint on the user-facing auth surface is ADMIN-only. The capability constant SECURITY_SESSION_REVOKE_OWN is defined in membership-capability.resolver.ts but is wired to no route, so it grants nothing. The staff plane is credited; the gap is the user plane.

conditions.condition: a highly sensitive money operation exists as a command
the path that executes it still asks for no further authentication
a wired further-authentication gate exists elsewhere, so the capability is real

decisions.note: Releasing funds is the most sensitive operation this platform performs, and the path that executes it asks for nothing beyond an already-authenticated session. The session must carry a verified second factor to exist at all, which is a real baseline, but the requirement asks for further authentication at the point of the operation and there is none: no fresh-MFA check, no step-up, no secondary verification anywhere on the command path. The capability is not missing from the platform - registration-decision.service.ts refuses a decision unless MFA was verified within 15 minutes - it is simply not applied where the money moves. Read together with V2.3.5, the money-release command has neither a second approver nor a re-authentication step.

conditions.condition: the platform acts as a relying party against an external identity provider
no session termination is propagated between relying party and provider

decisions.note: The platform is a relying party: it builds an authorization-code request with client_id, redirect_uri, scope openid, state and nonce. Nothing propagates session termination in either direction - no RP-initiated logout, no front-channel or back-channel logout, no logout_token handling - and no document describes what the behaviour should be. Both halves of the requirement are unmet.

conditions.condition: the federated flow is started by an explicit user action carrying anti-forgery state
the flow is disabled unless deliberately configured

decisions.note: A federated session is never created implicitly. The flow begins only from an explicit user action, carries a per-request random state and nonce in httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies with a ten minute lifetime, and is inert entirely unless the bridge is configured and enabled. A drive-by request cannot mint a session.

conditions.condition: function and data level restrictions are enforced in code and policy
no document defines the rules those restrictions implement

decisions.note: The restrictions themselves are strong and enforced in the database. What is missing is the statement of what they are meant to be: no document defines function-level or data-specific access rules, so an implementation cannot be reviewed against an intent. This is the same shape of gap as V2.1.x and V7.1.x, and it is the one place this otherwise strong chapter is consistently weak.

conditions.condition: no document defines field-level read or write restrictions

decisions.note: No document defines which consumer may read or write which field. Recorded separately from V8.2.3 because one is the missing rule and the other is the missing control; closing either alone would not close the other.

conditions.condition: no document defines environmental or contextual attributes for access decisions

decisions.note: No document defines time, location, device or any other contextual attribute as an input to access decisions. Consistent with V8.2.4, where no such control exists to document.

conditions.condition: no document describes how contextual factors enter authorization decisions

decisions.note: Nothing describes how environmental or contextual factors would be weighed, because none are used. The requirement is unmet rather than inapplicable: the platform makes access decisions, it simply makes them without these inputs and without saying so.

conditions.condition: authentication is a global guard rather than a per-route opt-in
the guard refuses a request without a bearer token
the public escape hatch is refused for sensitive flags in production

decisions.note: Function-level access is deny by default: AppAuthGuard is registered as a global APP_GUARD, so every route requires an authenticated consumer unless explicitly marked public. What makes that real rather than nominal is the second half - the public escape is itself gated by an environment flag, and the guard refuses the sensitive public flags outright in production. A route cannot be opened up in production by flipping a variable. 45 of 54 controllers carry role or guard decorators on top of this.

conditions.condition: row policies decide on the bound subject where they exist
a tenant-bearing table still carries no row level security

decisions.note: Corrected twice, and the second correction reverses part of the first. Measured denominator: 40 Prisma models carry tenantId, 37 map to a table with ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and 3 have no policy at all - deal_events, fgis_grain_tenant_read_provider_claims and fgis_grain_tenant_read_audit_heads. The two FGIS tables look missed rather than excluded: the same migration enables row level security on their siblings. deal_events is live - the authoritative command path reads and writes it inside the RLS transaction - but with no policy on the table the transaction-local tenant setting constrains nothing there. No cross-tenant read is exposed through it today: the one service that would read it filtered by dealId alone, DealEventService, has no reference outside its own file and is registered in no module. deal_events is not unprotected either - the industrial transaction core migration enforces append-only on it - but append-only is an integrity control, not a tenancy control. The earlier version of this note then said: where a policy exists, data-specific access is decided per row by PostgreSQL from the authenticated subject, and that part is strong. That sentence was wrong, and it was wrong in the way this programme keeps finding: it described the database CI builds, not the database a deploy builds. PostgreSQL combines permissive policies with OR, and 0001_postgresql_initial installed three policies granted to PUBLIC whose qualifier is literally true - deals_app_access on deals, audit_select_all on audit_events and ledger_select_all on ledger_entries. Their DROP statements existed only in infra/sql/production-rls-policies.sql, which no deploy path applies: only CI, the rehearsal script and the production-like acceptance harness reference it. On a migration-only database deals_app_access therefore ORs away the strict deals_select installed by 20260712193000, and on the other two the permissive SELECT is the only SELECT policy present. The repository had already articulated this exact principle for a different table - 20260807006000 says the boundary must be part of the forward-only migration chain and not an accidental property of a later deploy artifact - and the same reasoning had not been applied here. The distinction that makes the finding precise is the grantee, not the qualifier: this schema has around sixty policies written as FOR SELECT TO some_narrow_role USING (true), where the role is the boundary and the trivial qualifier is correct. Only a blanket policy granted to PUBLIC is a hole. audit_events and ledger_entries are closed by a migration in this pass and the class is now enforced by identity-rls-no-inert-policies.sql, which fails on any PUBLIC-granted policy whose every qualifier is true, with a source-controlled exclusion list carrying a reason per entry. deals remains excluded and open: closing it needs a deals_update policy, which exists only in the artifact, and the artifact has drifted from the chain in both directions - its deals_insert is broader than the narrowing 20260712195000 installed, and its deals_select is missing the app_deal_basis_deal_visible branch the chain has. Copying it would revert a deliberate tightening. Raised as #4814. This requirement stays FAIL: three tenant-bearing tables still carry no policy and deals still carries a blanket one.

conditions.condition: the access control that exists operates on rows
no field-level restriction exists alongside it

decisions.note: This is the requirement most at risk of being answered with the wrong evidence, so it is stated plainly: row level security restricts WHICH ROWS a consumer sees. It says nothing about WHICH FIELDS of a row they may read or write. No column-level grants, no field allowlists, no per-field write restrictions exist anywhere. The strength of the row-level control does not carry over, and treating it as though it did would be exactly the inference this mechanism exists to prevent.

conditions.condition: no adaptive control reads time, location or device as an access input

decisions.note: No adaptive or contextual security control exists. The only geolocation reference in the application is a Permissions-Policy header that disables it. The requirement is unmet, not inapplicable - an application making authorization decisions could use these inputs and this one does not.

conditions.condition: authorization is enforced by a server-side global guard
and again below the service layer, in the row policies the forward-only chain actually installs - not in an artifact that no deploy path applies
the database layer does not yet cover every tenant-bearing table

decisions.note: Enforcement sits in two places a client cannot reach: a global server-side guard, and row policies inside PostgreSQL. Nothing an untrusted consumer controls participates in the decision, and that holds for this requirement, which asks that the rules be enforced at a trusted service layer rather than that the database cover everything. Evidence corrected a second time, and this correction is the point of the record: the condition below the service layer pointed at infra/sql/production-rls-policies.sql, which only CI, docker-compose and the rehearsal and acceptance scripts reference - no deploy path applies it. Measured rather than argued: stripping every CREATE POLICY out of the forward-only chain did NOT revoke this decision, while editing that inert artifact did. The check was revocable by what does not matter and not revocable by what does. It now reads the chain migration that installed the strict audit_events and ledger_entries policies precisely because the artifact was never applied, and the same measurement confirms it revokes on the chain and no longer on the artifact. The status does not move: this requirement asks where enforcement sits, and the global server-side guard satisfies that on its own. Note also that the artifact remains legitimate evidence for V8.1.1, which asks that authorization DOCUMENTATION define the rules - a document need not execute to be a document. Wording corrected earlier: the first version said the database layer "holds even if the service layer forgets". That is true for the 37 tenant-bearing tables with a policy and false for the 3 without, so the claim is now scoped rather than universal. The trusted-layer requirement is still met - the guard is global and the policies are real - while the coverage gap is recorded where it belongs, under V8.2.2 and V8.4.1.

conditions.condition: the access token carries no authorization value that could go stale
authorization values are read from the session row on each request

decisions.note: Changes apply immediately because there is nothing cached to apply them to. The access token carries only a type, a session id, a credential version and a subject - no role, no tenant, no capability. Every request re-reads role, membership status and organization status from the database. conditions.condition: the API states its algorithm allowlist on both signing and verification rather than inheriting a library default
both web verifiers still refuse any header algorithm other than HS256

conditions.condition: the API issues a bounded lifetime and verifies it
the web verifier rejects an expired or not-yet-valid token

decisions.note: Access tokens carry a 15 minute expiry that jwt.verify enforces, and the web verifier checks both exp and nbf against the supplied time. A token outside its validity span is refused by both paths.

conditions.condition: the cabinet reader and the access-token reader each require the type the token was issued as
the API verifier still rejects a token whose type is not access
the commercial-surface verifier no longer treats an absent type claim as acceptable

The web cabinet reader checked no type at all and was handed the same JWT_SECRET the API signs access tokens with, so any HS256 token under that secret verified there; an access token yielded no cabinet role only because it carries no role claim, which is a behavioural accident rather than a check - adding one role claim to the access token, for any reason, would have turned the web tier into something that derives a cabinet role from a credential minted for the API. conditions.condition: the fixture contour still decides acceptance by audience and type together, not by a purpose flag

the staff page still requires its own audience
the owner cabinet route still requires its own audience
the API verifier still passes an audience to jwt.verify

decisions.note: Every service that accepts a self-contained token now accepts only tokens naming it. conditions.condition: the document most likely to be mistaken for a key management policy still exists and is still an exposure report
no document in the security set defines a key lifecycle

decisions.note: There is no key management policy. docs/security/SECRET_ROTATION_REGISTER.md is named so that a reader will reach for it here, so it is named explicitly: it is a secret-exposure scan report plus an incident procedure for what to do when a credential is found in Git. It defines no crypto-period, no custody rule, no limit on how many entities may hold a shared secret, and no alignment to a key management standard. Its own closing line says the inventory for material held outside Git "does not exist yet". The gap is the policy, not the capability - two subsystems already implement real key replacement (versioned outbox keys, bank keys with overlapping windows and database-backed revocation), and they do it without a written rule to implement. What that rule should say is an owner decision. Update: the owner has since approved a canonical data classification, which supplies the policy basis this requirement was missing on one side - C11_CRYPTO_SECRET now names what counts as key material and states that it is never logged, never sent to analytics, telemetry or an external model, and never carried in a query string. That is handling, not lifecycle. This requirement additionally asks for a key management standard, a crypto-period per key and a limit on how many entities may hold a shared secret, and none of those is decided. The verdict therefore does not change, and the remaining gap is now smaller and precisely stated rather than open-ended.

conditions.condition: the inventory is still generated from the tree rather than written by hand, and CI still fails when the committed copy goes stale
the usage map is still held to the generated inventory, in both directions and on the files each key appears in
the two key-separation violations found while building the map are still named in it rather than smoothed over

decisions.note: The earlier verdict rested on a fact that stopped being true: it said no cryptographic inventory exists. One does. scripts/security/discover-cryptography.mjs generates docs/security/cryptographic-inventory.json from the tree - operations with their algorithms and call sites, and twenty-seven named pieces of key material - and discover-cryptography.test.mjs fails CI when the committed copy goes stale, which is what makes it maintained and regularly updated rather than a snapshot someone took once. What the generated inventory could not answer is the second half of the requirement: where each key may and may not be used, and what data it may and may not protect. No scanner derives that, because it is a decision rather than a fact about the text. It is now recorded in docs/security/cryptographic-key-usage.json, one entry per key, and held to the generated inventory by verify-key-usage.mjs: the map must name exactly the keys the inventory found, each entry must list exactly the files the inventory saw it in, and an entry missing either half of its boundary fails. The consequence is the point - a key that spreads to a new file fails the build until someone revisits what that key is allowed to protect, which is the question this requirement is really asking. Building the map surfaced two key-separation violations, and both are named in it rather than smoothed away. The deal-registry pagination cursor fell back to signing with JWT_SECRET, the session-signing secret, with no domain separation; it was not exploitable, but only because a JWT signs a message containing a dot and a cursor signs one that cannot, so the safety came from message shape rather than key separation. Raised as #4790 and since closed: the cursor derives its own key by HKDF under pc-deal-registry-cursor:v1, the same form the opaque token authority already used, so the separation no longer depends on a coincidence of message formats and the fallback material can stay. And ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET is required by the API's env validation while no API code signs with it; only the web tier's commercial-surface reader verifies under it, and nothing in this repository mints such a token. Certificates: the application performs no certificate handling of its own - the only key of that kind in the inventory is the acceptance matrix's local TLS key, generated for the run - so TLS material at the edge is hosting configuration and is recorded as out of the application's custody rather than claimed as inventoried. The cryptographic key management POLICY this inventory would serve is a separate requirement and remains FAIL under V11.1.1: an inventory says what exists and what it is for, and a policy says what the lifecycle of that material must be. Nothing here is offered as the latter.

conditions.condition: the discovery mechanism still exists and still emits a versioned inventory
the generated inventory is still committed rather than produced and discarded
the guard that fails when the committed inventory goes stale is still present
CI still runs when the mechanism or its artefact changes

decisions.note: A repository-owned discovery mechanism now enumerates every instance of cryptography rather than reporting only the instances a security suite dislikes. It scans 2127 non-test source files under apps and packages, excluding apps/landing, and records encryption, decryption, hashing, MAC, three key-derivation families, password hashing, signature generation and verification, key-pair generation, key exchange, CSPRNG, UUID and non-CSPRNG randomness, constant-time comparison and WebCrypto - each with the algorithm, the call count and the files, and each reported as zero rather than omitted when absent. Key material is named and never read; a test asserts no key value can reach the artefact. Names that match the pattern but configure key material rather than being it - a keyring directory, a current-version pointer, a token budget - are labelled configuration rather than silently dropped, because discarding a match makes a list look cleaner than it is. The mechanism is employed rather than merely available: the artefact is committed, CI runs the scanner whenever it or its inputs change, and a test fails when the committed inventory no longer matches what the scanner produces, so it cannot rot into a one-off snapshot. The first run earned its keep immediately by finding two HMAC-SHA1 sites that the manual sweep behind this chapter had missed; see V11.4.1, whose note is corrected accordingly.

conditions.condition: the plan is still held to the generated inventory, so an algorithm cannot enter the tree without a stated way out
the plan still names every algorithm the generated inventory reports in the tree, so dropping one revokes this decision rather than only failing the gate
the plan still states a trigger, a target and a cost per algorithm and keeps its post-quantum position
patterns: what this plan does not cover

conditions.condition: the plan still refuses to be read as a key management policy

decisions.note: The inventory half of this requirement is answered under V11.1.2 - generated from the tree, held from going stale by CI, and now carrying a per-key usage boundary. What was missing was the plan, and it exists now as docs/security/CRYPTO_MIGRATION_PLAN.md. It is not prose left to age: verify-crypto-migration-plan.mjs derives the algorithm set from the generated inventory and fails when one of them is not addressed, when a trigger, target, cost or post-quantum position is missing, or when the plan carries fewer entries than there are algorithms - so a heading with nothing behind it does not count. An algorithm therefore cannot enter this codebase without someone deciding in advance how it would leave. Eight subjects are covered: AES-256-GCM, SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256, HMAC-SHA1, HKDF-SHA256, scrypt, bcrypt and the CSPRNG, plus the WebCrypto HMAC that moves with its Node counterpart. Each carries what it protects, why it stays, what would trigger a move, what it moves to, and what the move costs - and the costs are the part worth having, because they differ by an order of magnitude. scrypt migrates for free as users log in, since the stored format carries scheme, version and parameters and upgrades in place. HMAC-SHA256 is the expensive one: every opaque credential is stored as a digest that cannot be re-derived, so moving it means invalidating outstanding credentials, the same class of decision the owner settled in #4777 - and the existing v1 digest prefix is what makes a dual-accept window possible at all. HMAC-SHA1 is named rather than hidden: it is one site, it is TOTP, RFC 6238 specifies SHA-1, and its trigger is an ecosystem one - authenticator applications broadly supporting SHA-256 - not a cryptographic one; the property TOTP relies on is not collision resistance. The post-quantum position is stated first because it is the usual question, and it is measured rather than asserted: the inventory reports zero sites for signing, verification, key-pair generation and key exchange, so no asymmetric cryptography exists here and the Shor-shaped exposure lives in edge TLS, which is hosting configuration outside this repository's custody. What applies here is Grover, which halves symmetric strength rather than breaking it, and AES-256 and SHA-256 both retain a 128-bit margin. Harvest-now-decrypt-later is answered explicitly rather than skipped, and a test fails if those four operation counts ever stop being zero, because that is exactly when this section would silently become wrong. No dates are invented - every entry states a trigger, on the ground that a plan built on dates it cannot keep is a worse record than one built on conditions. The plan says what it does not cover, and a condition keeps it saying so: edge TLS, and key lifecycle, which is a key management policy and remains FAIL under V11.1.1.

conditions.condition: the hand-written JWT verifier still delegates the primitive to WebCrypto rather than implementing it
no re-implementation of cryptographic primitives is declared as a dependency

decisions.note: Every cryptographic primitive comes from node:crypto (OpenSSL), WebCrypto, or a published library - bcryptjs 2.4.3 and jsonwebtoken 9.0.3, both pinned in the lockfile. No primitive is re-implemented in the repository, and the eight manifests declare no JavaScript re-implementation of one. The one place that could be mistaken for hand-rolled cryptography is named rather than omitted: apps/web/lib/platform-v7/verified-session.ts parses and checks an HS256 JWT by hand instead of using a library. What is hand-written there is the envelope handling; the HMAC-SHA256 itself is crypto.subtle. Hand-written envelope parsing carries its own risks, which belong to V9, and this decision makes no claim about them.

conditions.condition: key replacement is implemented in the one subsystem that has it
the MFA envelope still rejects every key version but its own, so its version label is not a rotation path

decisions.note: Agility is real in two places and absent everywhere else, so the denominator matters. Key replacement: the auth-mail outbox holds versioned key files and derives per-version keys, and the bank callback registry accepts several keys at once with validity windows plus immediate database-backed revocation - those two can be rotated without downtime. The remaining key-holding subsystems hold one unversioned value each, so replacing the key invalidates every token or ciphertext already issued under it. auth-crypto is the case worth naming precisely: it stamps a v1 label into every MFA ciphertext and then rejects any other version on decrypt, so the label reserves a rotation path rather than providing one. Algorithm replacement: aes-256-gcm appears as a string literal at 15 call sites and sha256 at 95, none of them configurable, so changing a cipher or a hash means editing every site. Re-encryption of stored data has no mechanism outside the auth-mail outbox.

conditions.condition: the 32-character floor for configured secrets is still enforced and still fails closed in production
no cipher below 256-bit key length and no deprecated cipher is present

decisions.note: Every primitive clears 128 bits. AES-256-GCM is the only cipher present; SHA-256 is the only hash used cryptographically; HMAC-SHA256 and HKDF-SHA256 produce 32-byte outputs. Configured key material is floored at 32 characters by a central resolver that refuses to start a production process when a secret is missing or short, and the phone encryption key must decode to exactly 32 bytes or the service throws. No asymmetric key exists anywhere in the application, so the key-size question that this requirement illustrates with RSA and ECC does not arise here; that absence is machine-checked by the V11.1.4 and V11.6.1 conditions rather than assumed.

conditions.condition: one module still owns the bcrypt cost for the whole platform
both login paths still route the comparison through that module rather than choosing a fallback themselves
no file outside the owning module and the seed calls bcrypt hashing OR bcrypt comparison, so none can pick its own cost and none can assume the stored hash is bcrypt
the test that fails if the dummy and the stored cost diverge is still present
patterns: generates the dummy hash at the same cost as a stored password

decisions.note: Comparison of secrets is constant-time and the two login branches now do the same work. All 20 timingSafeEqual sites check length first or catch the length exception, which is the failure this pattern usually has. The work-factor gap recorded when this chapter was first assessed is closed at its cause rather than at its symptom: the cost was previously a literal in four writers plus two dummy-hash sites, and those drifted apart until the unknown-account dummy stood at bcrypt cost 10 against stored passwords at cost 12 - roughly a quarter of the work, so response time reported whether an email was registered. One module now declares the cost, derives the dummy from that same constant, and owns the branch itself: verifyPassword always performs exactly one comparison, against the stored hash when the account exists and against the dummy when it does not, so a future login path cannot skip bcrypt for a missing user or reach for a dummy of another cost. The conditions watch both login paths, the single declaration, the absence of any other caller of bcrypt hashing, and the test that fails if the two costs ever diverge again. One residue is stated rather than hidden: rows hashed before this change at some other cost keep that cost until their owner next sets a password, so existing accounts can still differ from each other. That is inherent to bcrypt without rehash-on-login and is a separate decision; what this requirement asks about - an artificial difference between the known and unknown branches - is gone. Rebound after V6.2.8: the condition that both login paths route the comparison through this module was written against the literal verifyPassword(, and both paths now call verifyPasswordWithUpgrade(, which is not a match for that substring. The check follows the call rather than being relaxed - the upgrading form calls verifyPassword internally, so the branch for a missing account, the dummy hash and the single comparison all still live in this module and neither login path chooses a cost or a fallback for itself. Had the pattern been left as it was, this decision would have been rejected rather than quietly passing, which is the intended direction: the login path moved, so the record had to be re-earned. Rebound a second time, back to verifyPassword(: the upgrading form was split into a plain verification plus a separate rewrite that runs after the login decision, so both paths call verifyPassword directly again. The property this requirement is about - one module owning the cost, the dummy hash and the single comparison - is unchanged by that split. A second hole in this requirement was found the same way the first one was - by a failing acceptance run, not by reading. The condition forbade every caller of bcrypt HASHING outside this module and said nothing about bcrypt COMPARISON, and organization-invitation.service.ts had two: confirmMfaRecovery and the invitation-acceptance password proof both called bcrypt.compare on the stored hash directly. That was already wrong before this pass and already breaking: hashPassword has written scrypt since the versioned scheme landed, so any account whose password was set after that point could not complete MFA recovery - bcrypt.compare against a scrypt record returns false and the flow reports MFA_RECOVERY_INVALID for a correct password. Rewriting legacy hashes on login turned that from a defect affecting new accounts into one affecting every account, which is how it surfaced. Both now call verifyPassword, and the condition names the comparison as well as the hashing so a third caller cannot appear.

conditions.condition: no padded block mode exists, so the padding-oracle class cannot arise
every decryption path still authenticates before returning plaintext

decisions.note: All six modules that decrypt use AES-GCM, and all six set the authentication tag before reading plaintext, so a modified ciphertext fails at final() and no plaintext is produced. There is no padded block mode anywhere in 3442 source files, so the padding-oracle class is structurally absent rather than merely unexploited. One asymmetry is named rather than smoothed over: decryptMfaSecret throws a distinguishable error for a malformed envelope and lets the GCM failure propagate separately, which would be an oracle if a caller could supply the ciphertext. It cannot - the value is read from the credential row in the database at both call sites - so the distinction is not reachable by an attacker. Every other decrypt path returns null for both cases.

conditions.condition: no insecure block mode is present in the tree
the approved mode is still the one in use at every cipher site

decisions.note: Every cipher instantiation in the repository is AES-256-GCM: 15 occurrences of the algorithm string across six modules, and no other algorithm string anywhere. GCM is an unpadded counter mode, so the weak-padding half of this requirement has nothing to attach to, and PKCS#1 v1.5 in particular cannot arise because no RSA operation exists. The denominator here is every createCipheriv and createDecipheriv call, not a sample: the two calls were enumerated first and each was read.

conditions.condition: AES-GCM is still the algorithm at every cipher site
no unapproved cipher has been introduced
no re-implementation of a cipher is declared as a dependency

decisions.note: AES with GCM is the example this requirement gives, and it is the only cipher the application has. The 1616 apparent matches for "des" in an earlier sweep were substring noise inside words such as "described" and "designed"; re-run with the algorithm string rather than the three letters, the count is zero. Nothing in the eight manifests provides a second cipher implementation that could be reached without a createCipheriv call.

conditions.condition: every encryption site still produces an authentication tag
every decryption site still requires that tag

decisions.note: Encrypted data is protected by an approved authenticated encryption method rather than by a separate MAC. Both halves are checked, because either alone would be misleading: all six modules call getAuthTag on encrypt and all six call setAuthTag on decrypt, so a tag is always produced and always required. Two of them go further and bind context that is not part of the ciphertext - the auth-mail envelope and the Gekta ticket both pass additional authenticated data - so a valid envelope cannot be replayed into a different purpose.

conditions.condition: every encryption site still draws a fresh 96-bit IV from the CSPRNG
no counter-based or fixed IV construction has been introduced

decisions.note: Each of the seven encryption operations generates its IV with randomBytes at call time, so no IV is reused across a key and data pair. Twelve bytes is the size GCM is specified for, which is the "appropriate for the algorithm" half of the requirement - a random 96-bit nonce is the standard construction for this mode, and none of the sites derives an IV from a counter, a timestamp or the plaintext. The auth-mail envelope additionally rejects any stored IV that is not exactly IV_BYTES long before attempting to decrypt.

conditions.condition: the authenticated mode that makes this ordering structural is still in use
no separate MAC is composed with a raw cipher, which is the case this requirement guards

decisions.note: The ordering is structural rather than chosen. No encryption algorithm is combined with a separate MAC algorithm anywhere; all six modules use GCM, which is AES in counter mode composed with GMAC computed over the ciphertext - that is encrypt-then-MAC by construction, and the mode does not offer the other orderings. This is recorded as a pass rather than as not-applicable because the property the requirement wants is present, not excused: on decrypt the tag is verified before any plaintext is returned, at all six sites.

conditions.condition: no MD5 hashing is performed by application code
the two SQL md5 calls still build a worker lease token and nothing else
the SHA-1 HMAC is still confined to the TOTP construction that specifies it

decisions.note: SHA-256 is the hash for every cryptographic purpose: digests, HMAC, HKDF and content integrity. MD5 is named here rather than left for a reader to find, because grepping the repository for it returns two hits and a silent pass would look like a miss. Both are PostgreSQL md5() calls that build a worker lease token from random() and clock_timestamp(), and both were followed to their use: the token is matched in the UPDATE guard that stops two workers claiming the same row. It is a concurrency token, not a secret, a credential, a signature, a key derivation or a random-bit generator, so it is not a cryptographic use and MD5 collision resistance is irrelevant to it. The single createHash("sha1") in the tree is negative test data inside a CodeQL model test asserting that the model flags it. Correction, found by the cryptographic discovery mechanism added under V11.1.3 rather than by the manual sweep behind this chapter: the claim that SHA-256 is the hash for every cryptographic purpose was incomplete. One runtime site uses HMAC-SHA1: the TOTP code generator in auth-crypto. The note said two until #4688 removed the decorative MFA module, which carried a second RFC 6238 implementation; the count is now taken from the generated cryptographic inventory, which reports mac: sha256 x22, sha1 x1, rather than from a sweep that has to be repeated by hand to stay true. That is not a defect and the verdict does not change: RFC 6238 specifies HMAC-SHA1 for TOTP, every authenticator application implements it, and HMAC does not rest on the collision resistance that SHA-1 has lost, so HMAC-SHA1 remains approved for this use where bare SHA-1 would not be. It is recorded here because a reader who greps for sha1 will find it, and an assessment that did not mention them would look like one that missed them - which, until the mechanism ran, it had. The platform used to carry two independent TOTP implementations; the second was removed in #4688 and a test in the auth module now fails if a second verifier reappears.

conditions.condition: stored passwords are still written with bcrypt at cost 12, declared once
the seed no longer chooses its own weaker cost
the test that fails if the cost drops below the current floor is still present
patterns: keeps the cost at or above the current owasp floor for bcrypt

decisions.note: Every path that stores a user password uses bcrypt at cost 12, and the cost is now declared in one place instead of four. Cost 12 is above the current OWASP floor for bcrypt, so the parameter meets guidance rather than merely being non-zero, and a test asserts that floor so a future reduction fails rather than passing quietly. The distribution that was recorded when this chapter was first assessed is no longer split: the canonical test deal seed previously wrote at cost 10, which left a seeded account distinguishable by the same measurement that V11.2.4 is about, and it now takes the shared constant like every other writer. bcryptjs 2.4.3 remains the implementation; no cryptography was written for this.

conditions.condition: the credential digest is still SHA-256 rather than a shorter hash
no non-test source file uses a hash shorter than 256 bits

decisions.note: Every hash used for data authentication or integrity is SHA-256, which is 256 bits and therefore clears the collision-resistance bar rather than only the second-preimage bar. The uses were followed individually: the raw body digest that pins a regulatory message to its stored projection, the SHA-256 of an API key that is stored in place of the key, and the digest that pins the ASVS source document this matrix is built from. No digital signature exists in the application, so the signature half of this requirement has no instance; that absence is machine-checked under V11.6.1 rather than assumed here. The second condition deliberately excludes test files. The one createHash("sha1") in the repository is an assertion inside a CodeQL model test that the model flags exactly that call, so a tree-wide absence check would contradict a fixture whose whole purpose is to contain the thing being forbidden.

conditions.condition: no user-supplied password reaches any key derivation site
the key material those sites do derive from is still floored at 32 characters

decisions.note: This requirement is scoped to keys derived from passwords, and no such derivation exists. Passwords reach bcrypt for verification and nothing else; the four key derivation sites take configured secrets or key files, floored at 32 characters and fetched from the environment or a key file, never from a login form. Key stretching is therefore the wrong control for these inputs - stretching buys time against guessing a low-entropy secret, and these inputs are not low-entropy. Two of the derivations are named so they are not mistaken for an omission: mfa-login-ticket and auth-crypto derive their key with a single SHA-256 pass rather than HKDF. That is adequate for a high-entropy input but provides no domain separation between purposes, which is recorded as part of the agility gap in V11.2.2 rather than treated as a password-stretching failure here.

conditions.condition: credentials are still generated from the CSPRNG at 256 bits
the demo generator is still refused before it runs in production
the controlled-test generator is still refused before it runs in production

decisions.note: The claim is scoped: every value intended to be non-guessable on a production-reachable path is generated by a CSPRNG with at least 128 bits. Counting Math.random alone would have measured the wrong set, because ASVS 5.0 states that UUIDs do not satisfy the 128-bit condition and randomUUID carries 122. So all three generator classes were enumerated - 47 randomBytes, 306 randomUUID, 50 Math.random - and the latter two were each examined for use as a secret. Exactly two sub-128-bit generators produce a value meant to be unguessable: a CSRF token from Math.random in the demo instant-login route, and a CSRF token from randomUUID in the cabinet lock login. Both sit in handlers that return before reaching that line when NODE_ENV is production, one of them behind a second opt-in flag as well, and the demo route session token beside it is an unsigned literal, so nothing there is a credential in the first place. The remaining Math.random sites are record identifiers, idempotency keys that need uniqueness rather than unpredictability, retry jitter, mock handlers and load-test fixtures. The near-miss is recorded: partner-api.service.ts builds its record id with Math.random on the line after the API key itself, which is randomBytes(32) hex, SHA-256 hashed before storage.

conditions.condition: no user-space pseudo-random generator or entropy pool exists in the tree
no seedable random library is declared as a dependency

decisions.note: The application operates no random number generator of its own. Every non-guessable value comes from node:crypto, which draws from the OpenSSL DRBG seeded by the operating system, and there is no application-level entropy pool, no seeding, no caching of random material and no fallback that would degrade to a weaker source when the CSPRNG is slow - randomBytes throws rather than returning low-quality bytes. That is what makes behaviour under heavy demand a property of the platform rather than of this code, and the conditions check the negative that makes it so: 3442 source files and eight manifests contain no seedable generator that a load-shedding path could fall back to.

conditions.condition: no signature or key-pair operation exists in application code

decisions.note: Key generation is randomBytes from the OS CSPRNG - the partner API key is randomBytes(32) rendered as hex - and configured key material is validated for length before use, so no key generation algorithm capable of producing a weak key is involved. An earlier draft of this note claimed that "verified: true" appears only in a type definition; that was wrong as written, because the string also occurs inside names such as mfaVerified, and the claim now rests on the caller check instead.

decisions.note: Two backend components that do not share the application’s session mechanism are reached without authentication, or with authentication that silently disappears if a variable is unset. patterns: must use a different postgresql principal

decisions.note: The staff-access boundary is a real least-privilege control, not an aspiration. STAFF_DATABASE_URL, AUTH_DATABASE_URL, DATABASE_URL and STORAGE_DATABASE_URL are each required to carry a distinct PostgreSQL principal - principalFromUrl() extracts and compares them, and the service throws if the staff principal collides with any other, rather than logging a warning and continuing. A companion inspection query checks the connected principal for superuser, bypass_rls, create_db, create_role and direct runtime-table privileges. Under shouldEnforceDatabasePrincipalBoundary(), a strict acceptance and production path cannot start without a distinct STAFF_DATABASE_URL at all. This is the pattern the rest of V13.2 is measured against, and it is why the other findings in this chapter read as gaps rather than as an unreachable bar.
